title: Classic Maya period
summary: From about 250 to 900 CE, rival dynasties of divine lords ruled dozens of Maya city-states in the tropical lowlands of Mesoamerica, raising stone stelae dated in the Long Count, before most southern cities were abandoned.
card: The Classic period is the era of dated royal monuments in the Maya lowlands of today's Guatemala, Mexico, Belize and Honduras, conventionally c. 250–900 CE. Kingdoms such as Tikal, Calakmul's Kaan dynasty, Copán, Palenque and Caracol fought, allied and recorded their histories in hieroglyphic texts. Lidar suggests millions of people lived there in the eighth century; by around 1000 CE the southern cities stood largely empty, after drought, war and economic change.
what:
The Classic period is the span in which lowland Maya kings recorded their reigns on carved stone monuments dated with the Long Count calendar. A chronology following Coe (1987) places it from about 250 to 900 CE, with a Late Classic peak from about 600 to 800; other scholars write 300–900 or 300–1000 CE, so both boundaries are conventions rather than events. Tikal's earliest dated sculpture, Stela 29, carries a date in 292 CE and its last, Stela 11, one in 869; the latest Long Count date on any monument, at Toniná in Mexico, falls in 909.

Political life centred on kingdoms ruled by divine lords. Tikal (Mutal) in Guatemala's Petén records 33 rulers. In 378 CE a figure named Sihyaj K'ahk', linked to the central Mexican metropolis of Teotihuacan, arrived at Tikal on the day its king died, and a new line took the throne; whether this was a conquest is still argued. A lord from the Tikal region founded Copán's 16-ruler dynasty in 427. From the sixth century the Kaan (snake) dynasty, later seated at Calakmul, built a rival network: Tikal was defeated in 562 and fell silent for some 130 years, Palenque was attacked in 599 and 611, and Tikal answered by defeating Calakmul in 695. Women sometimes held power: Lady Yohl Ik'nal ruled Palenque for 21 years before the long reign of K'inich Janaab Pakal (615–683).

The 2016 lidar survey of northern Guatemala mapped 61,480 structures and implies 7–11 million people across the central lowlands in 650–800 CE, with causeways, wetland field systems, upland terraces and defensive earthworks. During the Terminal Classic, about 800–1000 CE, the southern cities lost their kings and most of their people. Scholars disagree on why: some give drought the leading role, others stress warfare, land degradation and a shift of trade to coastal sea routes. Dates here use the Goodman–Martínez–Thompson correlation; its variants (584283, 584285, 584286) differ by a few days.

uncertainty.note: Period boundaries are scholarly conventions: 250–900 CE (Coe 1987 chronology), 300–900 CE (Kennett et al. 2013; UNESCO Copán listing), 300–1000 CE (Kennett et al. 2012), Classic 300–800 plus Terminal Classic 800–1000 CE (Turner & Sabloff 2012). All Long Count conversions depend on the GMT correlation; the 584283 and 584285 constants differ by two days, so a date such as 8.17.1.4.12 is 14 January 378 (584283) or 16 January 378 (584285) in the proleptic Gregorian calendar (13 or 15 January Julian). Skidmore (2010) gives Palenque dates in the Julian calendar under 584285; Kennett et al. (2013) give 6 August 695, which is Gregorian under 584283.

how: The Classic order rested on three foundations. First, a farming landscape engineered at scale: lidar shows about 362 km² of deliberately modified farmland in the surveyed area, wetland field systems that imply central planning, upland terraces managed by households, and some 106 km of causeways linking settlements. Second, divine kingship expressed in writing and calendars: rulers commissioned stelae, lintels and stairways whose texts used the Long Count, a day count from a base date of 13.0.0.0.0 4 Ajaw 8 Kumk'u, and by 600–900 CE this practice had spread to more than 40 lowland centres. Third, a competitive political system in which dynasties made patron–client alliances and fought: the Kaan kingdom built a network of allies against Tikal, Caracol's K'an II fought Naranjo as its ally, and defensive earthworks spread across the landscape. Climate set the stage. A stalagmite record from Yok Balum Cave in southern Belize shows unusually wet conditions from 440 to 660 CE, matched by population growth and more political centres, then a long drying trend from 660 to 1000 CE marked by fragmentation and more warfare. Gypsum from Lake Chichancanab implies that annual rainfall fell by 41–54% during the Terminal Classic droughts. Heavy forest clearance, soil erosion and scarce fuel and timber added stress, while long-distance trade shifted to sea routes around the Yucatán Peninsula, draining wealth from the inland kingdoms. As kings failed to deliver, people left the southern cities over the ninth and tenth centuries.
why_it_matters: The Classic Maya kept a written, dated political history. Because their monuments carry Long Count dates, and radiocarbon dating of a Tikal lintel has confirmed the standard correlation with the European calendar, events at Tikal, Palenque or Copán can be placed on a single day. The texts give names and deeds to individual kings and queens, including women such as Lady Yohl Ik'nal who ruled in their own right, and the 1952 discovery of Pakal's tomb at Palenque counts among the greatest finds of Mexican archaeology. The lidar results changed the picture of tropical civilisation: a forest long assumed to support only scattered farming held an estimated 7–11 million people, linked by causeways and fed by engineered fields. The period's end is just as consequential. Population in the central lowlands fell by close to 90%, and the region stayed largely empty for more than a thousand years; old-growth forest returned within a few centuries, and Tikal and Calakmul now lie in the Maya Forest, the second-largest expanse of tropical forest in the Americas. Turner and Sabloff find that the interior was never reoccupied, even after forests and soils recovered, because once trade had turned to the coasts it offered no commercial advantage; had trade stayed inland, the Petén might well have filled again. The collapse is now studied as a case of how drought, land use and economic change interact, a lesson those authors explicitly draw for present-day sustainability.

292 CE: Tikal's earliest dated stela. Its kings will keep recording their reigns in stone until 869.
January 378: Sihyaj K'ahk', tied to Teotihuacan in central Mexico, arrives at Tikal the day its king dies; a new king takes the throne in 379.
427 CE: Yax K'uk' Mo', coming from the Tikal region, founds the dynasty that will give Copán 16 rulers.

perspectives.holder: Kennett et al. (2012), Science; Evans et al. (2018), Science
perspectives.account: Climate was a major driver: a wet interval (440–660 CE) favoured growth and political expansion, a drying trend from 660 CE accompanied fragmentation and warfare, and Terminal Classic droughts cut annual rainfall by about 41–54% (up to 70% at peak), stressing maize farming.

The collapse was a coupled human–environment process: deforestation, erosion and fuel scarcity, amplified by aridity, interacted with intercity conflict and, most importantly in their view, a shift of trade to sea routes around the peninsula; people moved away for better opportunities, and there is little evidence of mass famine.

perspectives.holder: Canuto et al. (2018), Science (PACUNAM Lidar Initiative)
perspectives.account: Widespread, sizeable defensive features in the lidar data point to societal disconnection and large-scale conflict, giving warfare a larger structural role in the Late Classic landscape than earlier site-based surveys showed.

perspectives.holder: David Stuart (1998 extract; UT Austin 2020); many archaeologists per UT Austin
perspectives.account: Sihyaj K'ahk' came from or on behalf of Teotihuacan, possibly with an army, and his arrival in 378 coincided with the death of Tikal's king and the installation of a new dynasty; Stuart proposes that Spearthrower Owl was Teotihuacan's ruler. The conquest reading remains debated, and Stuart himself flagged parts of it as speculative.

perspectives.holder: Martin and Skidmore (2012); Kennett et al. (2013)
perspectives.account: The Goodman–Martínez–Thompson family of correlations is accepted; 584283 and 584285 are the most widely used constants, Martin and Skidmore argue for 584286, and radiocarbon dating of Tikal Temple I Lintel 3 strongly supports the GMT family while ruling out constants centuries away.

importance.justification: The Classic Maya period is the best-documented civilization of the pre-Columbian Americas, with an independent writing system and day-precise dated history, and a seed anchor that must be visible at whole-planet view.

reviewer_note: Least sure of the period boundaries (250 vs 300 start; 900 vs 1000 end are conventions), the conquest reading of the 378 entrada, and the 562 victor (Martin 2005 favours the Kaan ruler Sky Witness but calls it unproven); Kennett 2012 was read only as its abstract record and press release.
